title: LeDeR: learning from lives and deaths
blurb: Explain what LeDeR is, quote the republished 2023 findings accurately and turn them into safer everyday practice.
question: Harry, 52, who had a learning disability, has died in hospital after a chest infection was recognised late. His supported living nurse asks what LeDeR is and whether his death should be notified. What is the best answer?

teach.body: LeDeR, 'Learning from lives and deaths: people with a learning disability and autistic people', is an NHS England service improvement programme. It reviews the lives and deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people to find what could be done better, then drives changes in local services. National reports are written by King's College London. In plain English: LeDeR looks back at each death to stop the next avoidable one.
teach.cite: NHS England LeDeR; KCL LeDeR 2023 report (republished Jan 2026)

teach.body: Harry, 52, had a learning disability and died after a chest infection was recognised late. His nurse notifies LeDeR (anyone can, including family and staff) and reports the delay through the incident system so the hospital can learn too. She shares what she knew of Harry's usual self and his support. A LeDeR review is not about blame: it asks what in Harry's life and care could have been better, so others with a learning disability do not die avoidably.

rows.label: Pneumonia
values: Spot dysphagia, act early on chest signs

teach.text: The 2023 report was withdrawn in December 2025 and republished on 27 January 2026. Do not quote older summaries of it: use the republished figures (average age 63, 58 with severe or profound LD, about 4 in 10 adult deaths avoidable). And LeDeR covers autistic people as well as people with a learning disability.

items: LeDeR: NHS England service improvement programme reviewing deaths of people with LD and autistic people.
2023 (republished Jan 2026): 3,556 deaths; average age 63; 58 with severe or profound LD.
About 4 in 10 adult deaths avoidable; top causes cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, heart problems.
Ethnicity gap, earlier diabetes and bowel cancer, constipation, missing adjustments and delays.

summary: You can now explain what LeDeR is and who it covers, quote the republished 2023 figures correctly, and link its findings to practical nursing actions. You also know that anyone can notify a death.

A.q: Amara is a newly registered learning disability nurse. Harry, 52, whom she supported, has died in hospital. Her manager says his death will be 'notified to LeDeR'. Which best describes LeDeR?
options: A coroner's inquest held into every death of a disabled person
A service improvement programme that reviews deaths to learn
A disciplinary process for staff involved in a death
A national register used to plan social care budgets
A.why: LeDeR is an NHS England service improvement programme that reviews the lives and deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people to improve services.

whyNot.0: Inquests are held by coroners in certain deaths; LeDeR is separate.
whyNot.2: LeDeR is about learning and improvement, not discipline.
whyNot.3: LeDeR is not a budgeting register.

A.q: Samuel, a staff nurse, is supporting the family of Daniel, 34, an autistic man without a learning disability who has died after a short illness. The family ask if LeDeR covers Daniel. What is the correct answer?
options: No, LeDeR reviews deaths of people with a learning disability
No, autistic adults are reviewed by the mental health trust
Yes, LeDeR reviews deaths of autistic people as well
Yes, if a psychiatrist confirms autism after death
A.why: LeDeR covers people with a learning disability and autistic people, as its full name states.

whyNot.0: Autistic people without a learning disability are included.
whyNot.1: There is no such separate mental health trust review in place of LeDeR.
whyNot.3: No post-death psychiatric confirmation is required.

A.q: During team teaching, Kofi presents the republished (January 2026) LeDeR report on deaths in 2023. Which were the most common causes of death?
options: Epilepsy, choking on food and sepsis from infection
Dementia, stroke and injuries from falls at home
Cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, and heart problems
Constipation, dehydration and accidental injuries
A.why: The republished 2023 report lists cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, and heart problems as the most common causes.

whyNot.0: These occur but were not the three most common causes.
whyNot.1: These were not the leading causes in the report.
whyNot.3: Constipation still contributed to deaths, but these were not the leading causes.

B.q: A student reads the republished 2023 LeDeR report. What was the average age at death of people with a learning disability whose deaths were notified in 2023?
options: About 63 years
About 58 years
About 71 years
About 52 years
B.why: The republished report gives an average age at death of 63 (62 in 2022).

whyNot.1: 58 was the average for people with a severe or profound learning disability.
whyNot.2: 71 is not the figure in the republished report.
whyNot.3: 52 is not the figure in the republished report.

B.q: Priya is briefing her ICB on the republished 2023 LeDeR report. Which figure describes the average age at death of people with a severe or profound learning disability?
options: About 63 years
About 66 years
About 49 years
About 58 years
B.why: People with a severe or profound learning disability died younger, at an average age of 58.

whyNot.0: 63 is the average for all people with a learning disability in the report.
whyNot.1: 66 is not the figure in the republished report.
whyNot.2: 49 is not the figure in the republished report.

B.q: Which statement about avoidable deaths in the republished 2023 LeDeR report is accurate?
options: About 1 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 4 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 7 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
About 2 in 10 adult deaths were rated avoidable
B.why: The republished report rates about 4 in 10 adult deaths as avoidable.

C.q: Lee, 45, who had a moderate learning disability, died on a surgical ward after a bowel obstruction was recognised late. A healthcare assistant asks whether only a doctor can notify LeDeR. What is the most appropriate action for the nurse?
options: Leave notification to the consultant who certified death
Wait for the coroner before deciding on notification
Ask the family to notify, as staff should not
Notify LeDeR and report the delay through the incident system
C.why: Anyone can notify LeDeR. The delayed diagnosis should also be reported through the incident system so local learning happens alongside the review.

whyNot.0: Notification is not restricted to doctors.
whyNot.1: LeDeR notification does not wait for the coroner.
whyNot.2: Families can notify, and so can staff.

C.q: An ICB is reviewing local LeDeR data alongside the republished 2023 national report. Which national finding about ethnicity should it expect to explore?
options: People from Black, Asian or mixed backgrounds died younger
People from White backgrounds died younger than others
Ethnicity made no difference to age at death
Ethnicity was not recorded in the national report
C.why: The republished report found that people from Black, Asian or mixed ethnic backgrounds died younger.

whyNot.2: The report did find differences by ethnicity.

C.q: A practice nurse is planning annual health checks after reading the republished 2023 LeDeR report. Which finding most directly supports earlier attention to diabetes risk?
options: Diabetes was the leading cause of death in 2023
Diabetes affected people 10 to 15 years earlier
Diabetes was less common than in the general population
Diabetes deaths were mainly in people over 75
C.why: The report found diabetes affected people with a learning disability 10 to 15 years earlier, supporting earlier screening and prevention at annual health checks.

whyNot.0: Cancer, pneumonia and heart problems were the leading causes.
whyNot.2: The finding was earlier onset, not lower frequency.
whyNot.3: The report emphasised earlier onset, which is inconsistent with this.

reteach.title: Three numbers and three causes
reteach.question: What is the minimum you must remember about LeDeR for practice and the exam?

blocks.body: Average age at death 63. With severe or profound learning disability, 58. About 4 in 10 adult deaths avoidable. The top causes were cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, and heart problems. These come from the republished January 2026 report on deaths in 2023.

blocks.text: Anyone can notify LeDeR, and it includes autistic people. It is about learning, not blame.

explain.body: LeDeR is an NHS England service improvement programme reviewing the lives and deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people. Anyone can notify a death.

test.q: Who can notify the death of a person with a learning disability to LeDeR?
options: The GP who knew the person best
The consultant who certified death
Anyone, including family and staff
The coroner after an inquest
test.why: Anyone can notify a death to LeDeR, including family members and staff.

whyNot.0: GPs can notify, but so can others.
whyNot.1: Consultants can notify, but so can others.
whyNot.3: Notification does not depend on a coroner or inquest.

explain.body: The 2023 report was first published in September 2025, withdrawn in December 2025 because of data errors, and republished on 27 January 2026. Use the republished figures.

test.q: A nurse is citing figures from the LeDeR report on deaths in 2023. Which version should she use?
options: The version published in September 2025
A news summary of the withdrawn report
The 2022 report, as the 2023 one was withdrawn
The version republished in January 2026
test.why: The 2023 report was withdrawn because of data errors and republished on 27 January 2026; the corrected figures should be used.

whyNot.0: The September 2025 version contained data errors.
whyNot.1: Summaries of the withdrawn version may contain incorrect figures.
whyNot.2: The 2023 report has been republished and is the current source for 2023 deaths.

explain.body: 3,556 deaths notified; average age 63; severe or profound LD 58; about 4 in 10 adult deaths avoidable; top causes cancer, pneumonia and lung infections, heart problems.

test.q: According to the republished 2023 LeDeR report, how many deaths of people with a learning disability were notified?
test.why: The republished report records 3,556 notified deaths of people with a learning disability in 2023.

whyNot.1: This is not the figure in the republished report.
whyNot.2: This is not the figure in the republished report.
whyNot.3: This is not the figure in the republished report.

explain.body: Recurring problems were missing reasonable adjustments, jargon and delays to tests and treatment. Nurses respond by planning adjustments in advance, acting early on chest and bowel signs and supporting accessible screening.

test.q: Local LeDeR reviews found that people waited weeks for blood tests because staff had not planned adjustments. What is the best change for a ward to make?
options: Ask families to arrange private blood tests
Check recorded adjustments and plan them before tests
Use sedation for all blood tests in this group
Refer every patient with LD to the liaison nurse to take bloods
test.why: Checking recorded adjustments (such as the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag and passport) and planning them before tests prevents the delays LeDeR identified.

whyNot.0: This shifts the duty to families and does not fix the service.
whyNot.2: Blanket sedation is restrictive and not an individual adjustment.
whyNot.3: Liaison nurses advise and support; the ward still needs to plan adjustments itself.
